creator_display_ssim: Dr. F. Krantz of Bonn, Rheinisches Mineralien-Kontor (estab. 1833), maker
description_tsim: Solid plaster cast of a partial Homo erectus skull. The original skull - initially named 'Pithecanthropus' by its discoverer - has been dated at between 700,000 and 2,000,000 years old and is the type specimen for this species. It was found by palaeoanthropologist Eugène Dubois in 1891 along the Solo River near Trinil in East Java, Indonesia. After its discovery, the identity and evolutionary place of Homo erectus was controversial, but is now generally accepted as a direct ancestor of modern humans. These casts were bought by the Anatomy Department in 1910 to use as teaching specimens in classes on human anatomy and evolution.

creator_display_ssim: R. F. Damon and Co (estab. 1850), maker
description_tsim: Plaster cast of a partial skull from a Neanderthal (Homo neanderthalensis). The original skull has been dated at ~40,000 years old and is the type specimen for this species. The skull was found in 1856 in a cave in the Neander Valley, a paleolithic fossil site in Germany for which this homin species was named. The discovery of this skull and the recogition that it represented a distinct, ancient species of extinct human marked a paradigm shift in scientific thinking. This cast was bought by the Anatomy Department in 1909 to use as teaching specimens in classes on human anatomy and evolution.
Left mandible of a domestic cow (Bos taurus). Cheek teeth and two incisors present. Pairs with 516-500457.

creator_display_ssim: Dr. F. Krantz of Bonn, Rheinisches Mineralien-Kontor (estab. 1833), maker
description_tsim: Plaster cast of a chimpanzee (Pan sp.) radius. The cast was manufactured by a commercial dealer in scientific specimens, Dr F. Krantz of Bonn, Germany. It was cast from an original specimen in the Berlin Museum of Natural History, accession no. A3909. This cast would have been used in anatomy classes in the 20th century to teach students about the anatomical and osteological evidence for the evolution of humans.

description_tsim: Large, robust vertebra from a domestic cow (Bos taurus).

Articulated pelvic girdle of a female common brushtail possum (Trichosurus vulpecula), comprising pelvic bones, epipubic bones, and six vertebrae (Sa1, Sa2, Cd1-C4). Specimen is articulated with dried tissues.

Thirteen humeri from a species of antechinus (similar in size to dusky antechinus, Antechinus swainsonii). Two humeri are significantly smaller and may belong to a different antechinus species. The bones are stained a reddish brown colour and have a translucent quality. Contained in a small glass vial - broken at the base - with a cork stopper. These are subfossil bones from Kelly Hills Caves on Kangaroo Island, South Australia, collected by Frederic Wood Jones on his May 1926 visit to the island and the caves.

Skull of a domestic calf (Bos taurus). The cranium is massively enlarged due to pathology or abnormality. The skull has been disarticulated into dozens of smaller pieces. Two maxillas and one mandible is present.
Partial skull of domestic dog (Canis lupus familiaris). Front half of skull missing.
Animal vertebra with tall dorsal projection.

Partial disarticulated skeletons of 3-4 individual common wombats (Vombatus ursinus). The bones comprise five scapulae, five femora, five humeri, four ulnae, three radii, six tibia, seven fibulae, and dozens of ribs and vertebrae. No cranial material. Ink inscription on box lid reads, 'PHASCALOMYS MITCHELLI VICTORIA SKELETONS (INCOMPLETE) 9.2.233A'. Phascolomys mitchelli is a now superceded scientific name for the common wombat. The Hunterian Museum in the Royal College of Surgeons, London hold a skull associated with these bones (RCSOM/A 363.59), also labeled with the code 9.2.233.
source_reference_tsim: 9.2.233A, Wood Jones number

creator_display_ssim: R. F. Damon and Co (estab. 1850), maker
description_tsim: Plaster cast of a partial human mandible from an incomplete skeleton of an adult male found in 1883 during the construction of new docks at Tilbury, Essex, on the north shore of the Thames. At the time the find stirred considerable interest due to its depth of nearly 10m, and anatomist Richard Owen thought it was likely to be paleolithic in age. However, radiocarbon dating has shown the skeleton dates from the late mesolithic, around 6,000 years BC. These casts were bought by the Anatomy Department in c.1909 to use as teaching specimens in classes on human anatomy and evolution.

creator_display_ssim: Dr. F. Krantz of Bonn, Rheinisches Mineralien-Kontor (estab. 1833), maker
description_tsim: Plaster cast of a mandible fragment from a Neanderthal (Homo neanderthalensis), including left lateral incisor, left canine, left first premolar, left second premolar and left first molar. This bone was part of a fossil assemblage discovered in Krapina, Croatia between 1899 and 1905. These Neanderthal fossils have been dated at 120-130 thousand years old and represent one of the largest assemblages of Upper Pleistocene human skeletal remains ever found. These casts were bought by the Anatomy Department in the early 1900s to use as teaching specimens in classes on human anatomy and evolution.

creator_display_ssim: Department of Anatomy and Physiology Teaching, The University of Melbourne, maker
description_tsim: 95 page catalogue of specimens on display in the Department of Anatomy's museum as of March 1976. It contains records for specimens numbered 1. to 512. This document was created for anatomy students to find specimens while in the museum. The catalogue opens with rules for using the museum and a description of the arrangment of the cabinets. The specimens are numbered from 1 onwards and a brief description is provided of each dissection. Some entries have the name of the prosector and the date the dissection was made. This catalogue dates from the era before the merger of the Pathology Museum and the Anatomy Museum.

creator_display_ssim: McCoy Society for Field Investigation and Research (estab. 1935, closed 1998), collector
description_tsim: Subfossil left coracoid from a goshawk (Accipiter sp.), medium-sized birds of prey in the family Accipitridae native to Australia. The coracoid is a paired bone of the pectoral girdle present in all all vertebrates except therian mammals (marsupials and placentals). The bone has been coated in wax; a museum technique of the early to mid-20th century used to stabilise fragile bones. This specimen was collected by the McCoy Society on their expedition to Bass Strait's King Island from December 1937 to January 1938.

Black and white photograph, mounted with cardboard and glass, of six Australian sea lions (Neophoca cinerea) in the ocean on Pearson Island, South Australia. Some overpainting with watercolours and pencil.

Subfossil posterior section of a partial left mandible of a southern hairy-nosed wombat (Lasiorhinus latifrons). The coronoid process has broken off and separated from the main mandible section. The bone is stained a chocolate brown colour. This mandible is from Kelly Hills Caves on Kangaroo Island, South Australia where the species is now locally extinct. They were collected by Frederic Wood Jones on his May 1926 visit to the island and the caves.

Calculus specimen two halves, polished. A calculus is a concretion of material, usually mineral salts, that forms in an organ or duct of the body. The concentric, radial in this calculus means it is likely a kidney stone formed from uric acid.

description_tsim: Amniocot and brochure for "Amni-Glove, The Amniotomy Glove". The amnicot is a small flat rubber disc with a hook used to rupture the membranes of the amniotic fluid and encourage labour. The absence of a fluid buffer between the fetus and uterus stimulates uterine contractions, which are also promoted by the rush of prostaglandins from the amniotic fluid.  The amnicot is sealed in the manufacturer’s plastic packaging which has a clear front plastic casing and paper backing. On the reverse of the packaging the following details are in black text: "AMNICOTS / (A new Instrument for Amniotomy ) / Latex Fingercots with Hook Attached / Sterile Disposable/ Position the amnicot over the pulp of the in / dex or middle finger of a gloved left or right / hand. Roll firmly over the finger, to hold / hook in position. / * Note the hook should point towards the palm of the hand. . . . ./ Manufactured by Go Medical Industries Pty. Ltd. / 20, Denis Street, Subiaco 6008, Western Australia / Telex AA93609, Fax (09) 382 4952 / Ph (09) 381 9195 / STER Date. Jan 89 / EXP. Date: Jan 94".    The brochure is colour printed in blue and black with white and black text.  The amnicot (A1993_06_106.1) measures 12.5 x 7.5cm  The brochure (A1993_06_106.2) measures 30.0 x 21.0cm

Physical description: A complete skull and mandible derived from an adult female thylacine (Thylacinus cynocephalus), in two parts. There is some fracturing between the parietal and the frontal bones on the posterior side of the right orbit. Multiple linear cutting marks are present on the frontal bone, possibly as a result of the skinning process. Bright blue paint marks have been applied to the left ascending ramus and the palate. Upper left M3 and lower left M3 have been removed and reattached with adhesive or putty and there is some loss of bone at this site.A small fragment of the skull has detached.  History: An old label from the Henry Forman Atkinson Dental Museum describes HFA3795 as, 'No. 6 Animal skull, thylacine. c. 1920. 10.0 x 12.0 x 19.0 cm. Comparative Anatomy Collection. Melbourne Dental School'. It is probable that this was the specimen from which Professor Charles Harold Down modelled the thylacine tooth models he made in the 1930s. The thylacine tooth models comprise four left lower third molars (HFA2420, HFA2880, HFA2914, HFA4011) and two left upper third molars (HFA2879, HFA4010). Down’s description of his methodology indicates that he had firsthand access to the teeth he was reproducing. The left upper third and left lower third molars - and no other teeth - of that specimen appear to have been removed and then glued back into the skull. HFA3795 was kept in the office of an academic from the Melbourne Dental School for some time in the 1980s and 1990s (R. Hardiman pers. comm. 2020, University of Melbourne).

credit_line_tsim: Gift of John Gibson, 2022
description_tsim: Practical dental metallurgy: a text- and reference-book for students and practitioners of dentistry, hardcover edition. This book covers the properties of metals commonly used in dentistry.  Joseph Dupuy Hodgen received his D.D.S. degree from the Dental Department of the University of California in November, 1887, he went to Woodland, where he entered practice with his father, who practiced some dentistry along with his medical practice. In 1891 he was appointed a member of the State Board of Dental Examiners by Governor Markham and remained a member and Secretary until December, 1897. In 1891, in response to an invitation from the faculty, he came to San Francisco to become Superintendent of the Infirmary, which position he held until 1894.  On January 26, 1892, he was appointed assistant to Professor Goddard in Dental Metallurgy, serving as Instructor in Chemistry and Metallurgy under both Dr. Goddard and Professor Lengfeld until 1900, when he was appointed, by the Regents, Professor of Chemistry and Metallurgy, which position he held until 1907. In September, 1896, he published the first edition of his Practical Dental Metallurgy. This book with revisions is now used in many dental colleges in the United States.  Guy S. Millberry graduated from Dental College of the University of California in 1901. Initially he set up in private practice in San Francisco, but within two years he returned to the University of California San Francisco to take the post of laboratory assistant in chemistry and metallurgy. In 1906  Guy Millberry came to the University fulltime as Superintendent of the Infirmary and acting Professor of Chemistry and Metallurgy. By 1910 he was promoted to Professor of Chemistry and Metallurgy, and by 1914 was named Dean of Dentistry. Interested in expanding public health with respect to dentistry, Dr. Millberry served  in the American Public Health Association, the American Association for the Advancement of Science, the California Academy of Sciences, the American Dental Association, and a number of dental honor societies. He published numerous papers on dental education and public health and was an editor of the textbook, Dental Metallurgy.

In 1728, Pierre Fauchard described the construction of dentures using a metal frame and teeth sculpted from animal bone. The first porcelain dentures were made around 1770 by Alexis Duchâteau. One of the most significant advancements for dental prosthesis in the 19th century was the development of vulcanite as a base for dentures. The lack of a durable and affordable denture base material (porcelain denture teeth were already developed). Swaged gold, and carved ivory were used but were expensive and only affordable to the rich. Vulcanite or “rubber” dentures became a popular base for dentures because of their durability, affordability, strength, elasticity, and lightness and were in widespread usage by 1863. “Vulcanite” in vulcanite dentures does not refer to the mineral vulcanite but rather hardened rubber obtained through a process called “vulcanizing”.

Ashworth (BA), F.C. Madden.  The seven women who entered the University of Melbourne’s Faculty of Medicine in 1887 were Misses Lilian Alexander MA, Elizabeth and Annie O’Hara, Helen Sexton, GraceClara Stone (called Clara), Grace Vale and Margaret Whyte. The women entered the school at the same time, but they did not graduate together. None were deliberately failed, but some had to miss a year through illness—one being Lilian Alexander, who commented, ‘I’ve studied so long that I am too tired to go on, I simply must have a rest before I continue withmy medical work’. Dr Clara Stone and Dr Margaret Whyte were the first graduates, in 1891,followed by Dr Helen Sexton and Dr Elizabeth O’Hara in 1892. Dr Alexander graduated in 1893, and Dr Annie O’Hara and Dr Grace Vale in 1894. Two other women joined the course—Misses Amy de Castilla( 1868-1898) and Emily Mary Page Stone(1865-1910), a cousin of Constance and Clara Stone—who graduated in 1893.

description_tsim: Alfred  George Fryett was born in 1862 in Lewisham London. After arriving Melbourne about 1893, Fryett was among the first to use X-rays in the late 1890s, assisting at the Melbourne Hospital. Fryett also worked with surgeon Fredric Dougan Bird at Clareton Hospital and with Harry Brookes Allen, Professor of Anatomy and Pathology in the University of Melbourne. In 1901 the University of Melbourne purchased X-ray equipment under the direction of Professor Allen. In 1902 Fryett was employed by Allen to prepare specimens with opaque injections and produce this collection of skigrams which display the aterirs throughout the human body. After Bird closed Claremont Hospital in 1914, Fryett returned to England and joined the R.A.M.C working as a radiographer at Lady Dudley's Hospital. The Sands and McDougall Melbourne Directories list Fryett as having his own radio-diagnostic business ," A.G. Fryett,  X-ray Department , 41 Spring St" from 1916 to 1919. In 1919 or 1920 Fryett returned to London, suffering health problems and retired in Malborough with his wife.  Fryett like many other pionerrs in this field became an x-ray ' martyr' dying in England in 1930, the result of 'carcinoma of the axillaand lung; epithelioma of hands; x-ray burns of fingers and hands'. Like other early radiographers or 'Skiagraphists', Fryett would often use his own  hands to test the strenght of x-ray beams, instead of using photometers that could easily be mislaid.  The collection of sterio skiagrams is Fryett's work in the Anatomy department, University of Melbourne from 1902 to c. 1914.

description_tsim: Photographic block for block printing. Subject is Old Medical School building (1864) in the 1870s, with artificial lake.  Melbourne Medical School’s first building, was situated on the north-eastern part of the campus across the lake from the rest of the University. The building was completed in  May 1864, designed by Messrs Reed and Barnes who also designed  Ormond College, the Baldwin Spencer Building and the original Wilson Hall as well as the State Library and the Melbourne Town Hall.  After 1885, when the new medical building of Anatomy and Pathology was built  alongside it,  the building became the Physiology department. The second storey was added in stages in 1900,1905, and in 1913 the portico was demolished.   The building  was demolished in 1970.  Used in a paper on the Medical School in 'M.J.A.'

description_tsim: Dr William Turton  (1762-1835) was a physician and naturalist. He matriculated from Oriel College, Oxford in 1781, graduating B.A., 1785. He obtained his M.A. in 1791 and his M.B. in the same year. He practised in Swansea and was particularily inerested in natural history. He was a prolific author, among his books: A medical glossary1797, British Fauna 1807, A conchological dictionary of the British Islands 1819, A treatise on hot and cold baths 1803, Bivalve shells of the British Islands 1830. He edited the General System of Nature (from Linnaeus) in 7 vols, 1802-06. He was a friend of Edward Jenner and being so impressed with Jenner's work on small -pox he named one of his daughters Vaccina ; she married James Mackin of Dublin and their son Charles Travers Mackin (1817-1884) was one of  the early doctors in Geelong.

Harry Brookes Allen (1854–1926) became the first Australian-born professor at the University of Melbourne in 1882, when a reform of the Medical School split the foundation chair of anatomy, pathology and physiology into two, with Allen being appointed professor of anatomy and pathology, and his teacher, the foundation professor George Britton Halford (1824-1910) retaining his first love, physiology. As well as serving as dean for extensive periods, Allen took on numerous positions as a medical administrator and government advisor, perhaps most importantly playing a major part in the introduction of Melbourne’s extensive sewerage system in the late nineteenth century. Dr Ross L Jones

description_tsim: Black and white photograph of Dr Lorna Lloyd-Green taken in the grounds of the University of Melbourne.  Lorna Lloyd-Green MBBS 1933 (1910–2002) was an inspirational leader in Australian Medicine during her 92 years. She graduated in 1933 and became one of Melbourne’s first female obstetricians and gynaecologists. Lorna was appointed medical superintendent at the Queen Victoria Memorial Hospital in 1939, and held various leadership positions there, including dean of the Clinical School. Motivated by her concern for those unable to have children, she founded the sterility clinic, which she ran for 25 years; eventually, this became the IVF clinic at Monash. Lorna was the first medical advisor to the then Nursing Mother’s Association and the first female fellow of the Australian Medical Association. She was also foundation fellow of the Australian College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists and president of the Australian Federation of Medical Women and the Medical Women’s International Association. Her honourable awards included an OBE (1968), Woman of the Year (1970) and CBE (1979). Lorna pioneered the way for women in medicine, with equal pay for equal work being one of her achievements. She was president of Zonta (Melbourne), a service that worked to advance the status of women, and she contributed to other organisations with this aim. She was renowned for her commitment to her patients: she never missed a delivery, and during World War II she was on call 24 hours a day for two years, spending every night in the hospital. Her sense of service was attributed to her family and school, Lowther Hall, where she was dux and captain (1929). A gifted musician, Lorna had considered becoming a music teacher. So, late in her career, when she felt it inappropriate to practise medicine,she re-trained as a music therapist, spending nearly ten years caring for dying patients, including a patient she had delivered 50 years before. Lorna had a lifelong passion for learning and studied for a Diploma in Law, using computers for the first time at the age of 80. An elegant, highly organised and energeticv woman, Lorna was also an ardent ecumenist, serving on the vestry and as church warden at St John’s Anglican Church in Toorak. Dr Lena Sanci MBBS 1988

credit_line_tsim: Gift of Australia Post, 2012
description_tsim: Commemorative postcard and postage stamp featuring a black and white photograph of Dr Dame Kate Campbell  on a blue background. Printed in black ink over both the postcard image and the postage stamp is a black stamp with the outline of a stethoscope and the text "First day of issue 10 April 2012 Healesville VIC 3777".  Dame Kate Campbell, DBE (1899-1986) was a physician and paediatrician and an eminent alumna of the University of Melbourne. After residencies at the Melbourne Hospital, Children's Hospital and (Royal) Women's Hospital, Campbell established a general practice and in 1929 began teaching neonatal paediatrics at the University of Melbourne - the first such appointment in Australia. A pioneer of neonatal intensive care, Campbell's most outstanding contribution in research was in 1951 when she established that excess therapeutic oxygen lay behind acquired retrolental fibroplasia, a condition that could lead to blindness among premature babies.  Appointed OBE in 1954, she was elevated to DBE in 1971 for services to the welfare of Australian children.

credit_line_tsim: Gift of Dr. John Andrew Brenan, 2012, great-great-nephew of Andrew Cairncross Livingston
description_tsim: Some of the first doctors to arrive in Australia from Europe were the ships’ surgeons. Initially accompanying the voyages of discovery to the new world, they then sailed on convict ships and later were part of many waves of immigration.  One of these surgeons was Dr Andrew Cairncross Livingston. Educated in Edinburgh, in 1852 he was surgeon superintendent (in charge of passengers) on the ship Una. He was paid ten shillings for every passenger delivered. The Una left Liverpool on 25 August 1852, arriving at Port Phillip seven months later, in February 1853.  The collection has his apprenticeship papers from 1828, degrees and medical registration certificates including the degree of doctor of medicine awarded by the University of Melbourne to Dr Andrew Cairncross Livingston (MHM2012.138). The testamur, signed by Chancellor Sir Redmond Barry and Vice-Chancellor A.C. Brownless, is dated 1858, four years before Brownless was successful in establishing a medical school at the University of Melbourne. It acknowledges the qualifications Livingston had received at the University of Edinburgh.

description_tsim: Black and white photograph of funnel-web spider specimens in jars with cotton wool. Funnel-web spider venom was a focus of the research by Dr Saul Wiener (1923 – 2010) whilst employed at the Commonwealth Serum Laboratories. The CSL issued appeals to the Australian public to send in spider specimens to aid in their research. In February 1957, a newspaper reported that Wiener hoped to develop the antivenom within six weeks. Two years later, however, Wiener admitted to the Melbourne Herald that research was “difficult because of the peculiar properties of the funnel-web spider’s venom.” The antivenom was eventually developed by Dr Struan Sutherland (1936-2002) and introduced in 1981. description_tsim: Dissection kit in leather wallet c.1950s made by W Ramsay ( Surgical ) Pty Ltd. 340 Swanston St, Melbourne. Used by , Judith Welch, in her Physiotherapy Diploma at the University of Melbourne  1951-1953.  Judith Elizabeth James (nee Welch) (b. Melbourne, 6 September 1933, died 12 September 2021) used this dissection kit as a student in the Diploma of Physiotherapy course at the University of Melbourne from 1951–1953. In 1952, the second year of her course, she excelled in the subject Anatomy (taught by Dr Marshall). In 1953, she graduated with the Australian Physiotherapy Association’s Josephine Jennings medal as the top student in the course. Judith then worked as a physiotherapist with expertise in paediatrics and disability at the Royal Children’s Hospital, Melbourne, in the 1950s and, later, with the Spastic Society of Victoria (now Scope). She also held positions at the Queen Victoria Hospital in the city as well as Maroondah Hospital in Ringwood East. In 1982, she graduated with a Bachelor of Science (Physiotherapy) from the Lincoln Institute of Health Sciences in Melbourne. All of this was accomplished while raising four children, two of whom went on to complete Arts/Law degrees at the University of Melbourne in the 1970s and 1980s respectively.

credit_line_tsim: Gift of Su Bradfield, 2021
description_tsim: Gilt metal circle glass lens spectacles with metal arms and spring hinge in black colour case.  Windsor eyeglasses were first produced in Britain in the 1840s, by the 1880s they were one of the most in demand eyeglass frames. They remained popular until the 1920s.  When they were first made in the mid-1800s, Windsor glasses had metal frames in gold, silver, and steel. The gold tone frames were often solid gold or gold filled. Celluloid (specifically Zylo) and plastic coatings for the frames became popular as the materials became available in later decades at which point colours and mock tortoiseshell patterns became more popular. Windsor circular glasses have perfectly round frames, a saddle bridge over the nose, and temples that extend back from the midpoint on the frames, they were generally relatively small on the face.  Unlike other shaped lenses that could only be remade by the initial manufacturer, round lenses from any brand could be a replacement in Windsor glasses  The production of true Windsor glasses fell out of fashion in the 1920s after the invention of nose pads. At this point, glasses similar in appearance, still often referred to as Windsors, incorporated nose pads and used a more gentle curvature in the temples since the additional stability was no longer needed.  From a collection of glasses formerly worn by Mrs M. Hassett (1891-1983) and her husband. The Glasses were worn from the early 1900s until 1983. They were originally obtained form optometrists in Warrnambool, Geelong, Ballarat and Melbourne, the most noted being Thomas Gaunt & Co. (Melbourne, Australia), late 19th century manufacturer and retailer of jewellery, clocks, watches and decorative items.

The container is formed by gathering strips of fronds of bull kelp into a bulbous cup shape to hold water. Held together with skewers made of tea tree.  Bull kelp containers or water carriers are a tradition of the Aboriginal people of the Furneaux Islands group off the north east coast of Tasmania (including the main islands of Flinders and Cape Barren) and the west coast of mainland Tasmania. Such carriers have been found to not only be a practical necessity for carrying drinking water, but to also be a health-related measure as Kelp contains high levels of iodine.  Eva (Auntie Eva) Richardson is one of a small group of elder artists in Tasmania today maintaining Tasmanian Aboriginal cultural traditions through visual arts practice. Eva Richardson, also known as Auntie Eva, was born in Moonah, Hobart, Tasmania. She is of the Trawlwoolway people of Cape Portland – Ben Lomond area of North East Tasmania.

description_tsim: Letter from Professor Halford to James Edward Neild, lecturer in forensic medicine from 1865 to 1904.  It was 1 May 1863 when George Britton Halford (1824–1910) started as the first professor of anatomy, physiology and pathology, at the Medical School. There were three students, Patrick Moloney (1843-1904), Alexander Mackie(1839-1892) and William Carey Rees (1843–1879), and classes were held in a shed erected at the back of Professor Halford’s private rooms.  In 1876 the faculty of medicine was established and took over administration of courses from the Medical School Committee. Halford was elected Dean and held office until 1886 and again in 1890-96.  Halford recommended as early as 1871, while president of the professorial board, that women who passed the relevant examinations sign the matriculation book should be admitted to the University of Melbourne. However, Vice-Chancellor A.C. Brownless’s (1817–1897) view of university education did not extend to the inclusion of women; he actively opposed the motion to admit women to the University of Melbourne in 1879, and to admit women to medicine in 1887.

description_tsim: Karl Pearson was born in London in 1857, studied mathematics at Cambridge, German literature in Berlin and Heidelberg, and law in London.  He was Professor of Applied Mathematics and Mechanics at UCL when he became interested in statistics as applied to biology and evolution through his collaborations with the zoologist W.F.R. Weldon.  Weldon introduced Pearson to Galton in the 1890s, and Pearson became an enthusiastic supporter of Galton's ideas on eugenics.  The three of them founded the journal Biometrika in 1901 as a vehicle for publishing the important developments in statistical theory they were making as they attempted to lay a scientific foundation for quantitative biology in general and eugenics in particular.  When Galton died in 1911 he left money in his will to the University of London to found a Chair in Eugenics, with the recommendation that Karl Pearson should be the first holder of the chair.  Pearson was duly appointed and founded the Department of Applied Statistics at UCL In 2021, University College London  expressed “deep regret” for its role in the propagation of eugenics, alongside a promise to improve conditions for disabled staff and students and a pledge to give “greater prominence” to teaching the malign legacy of the discredited movement.  The formal apology for legitimising eugenics – the advocacy of selective breeding of the population often to further racist or discriminatory aims – was UCL’s commitment to  address its links to early eugenicists such as Francis Galton, who funded a professorship in eugenics at the university.

description_tsim: The Medical Board for the district of Port Phillip in the colony of New South Wales  medical registration certificate issued to Dr. Edwin Stanford Maxwell.  Edwin Stanford Maxwell was  born, 8 September 1801, Island of Jersey, 2nd son of John Maxwell, who was serving in Army Medical Service and his 2nd wife, Ann Stanford. Maxwell qualified in midwifery in Dublin in 1827 and was admitted to MRCS in 1838.  Maxwell came to NSW in 1841 as surgeon on the ‘Adam Lodge’ and was living in Mulgoa. Returning to Ireland, he married Eleanor Bell in Londonderry 14 October 1847 where was in charge of the dispensary in Benburb, Co Tyrone. Maxwell with his wife and child returned to the Colony of Victoria on the “Eliza Caroline” which sailed from Plymouth on 31 December 1849 and arrived in Melbourne on 31 March 1850. Eleanor gave birth to their second child on the voyage. Maxwell  was employed on the ship as  the Surgeon Superintendent of 235 Irish girls who had been orphaned because of the Irish famine. There were no deaths on the voyage.  Maxwell  set up practice at 161 Collins St, Melbourne. In 1856, he  went to the goldfields to provide services as a doctor. In 1858 he was in Golden Square, Bendigo,where they lost 3 of their children as  infants in 1858,1860 and 1861. He was  public vaccinator at Seymour in 1867 and at Spring Creek in 1869. Moving to High St, Bendigo in 1973.  Maxwell was a  doctor in Victoria for 23 years and for 17 years served miners and families  on the goldfields. He became ill in 1874 and died on 24 February 1876. Surived by Eleanor and eight children.  Sources: NSW Medical Board. List of legally qualified practitioners. W. Baker 1842; NSW Medical Board register of medical practitioners 1869; Doctors and Digges on the Mount Eliza Goldfields KM Bowden 1974. description_tsim: This carbolic acid steam spray was used to disinfect an operating theatre. It is a later model of Joseph Lister's prototype, capable of developing a greater pressure of steam. It was owned by Surgeon Captain S J Lloyd.  British surgeon Joseph Lister(1827–1912) invented the spray based on his belief that carbolic acid could be used to destroy infectious germs in the operating theatre's atmosphere as well as around a patient's wound. Water was heated to boiling point in the upper chamber and steam was forced out of the thin tube. This was mixed with the carbolic acid in the glass container, forcing it into the air.
